title: Orzo: What It Is, Why It Looks Like Rice, and How to Cook It

seo.title: Orzo: What It Is, Why It Looks Like Rice, and How to Cook It
seo.meta_description: Orzo is semolina pasta shaped like rice, not rice itself. It can be boiled and drained like pasta, cooked directly in soup, or simmered with broth in a risotto-style method.
seo.search_intent: Understand what orzo is, why it is shaped like rice, what it is made from, and which cooking methods work best for different dishes.

excerpt: Orzo is small semolina pasta shaped to resemble a large grain of rice. The Italian word means “barley,” but the common modern product is neither barley nor rice. It can be boiled like pasta, cooked in soup, or simmered gradually with broth like risotto.
content_html:
Orzo is pasta shaped like a grain of rice. Classic orzo is made from durum-wheat semolina like many other dried pastas, even though its shape makes it easy to mistake for rice.

Barilla describes orzo as rice-shaped pasta and notes that the Italian word orzo means “barley.” That historical name adds another layer of confusion: the common supermarket product is neither rice nor barley.

Why does orzo look like rice?

Semolina-and-water dough is extruded or shaped into tiny elongated ovals. The small size allows the pasta to cook quickly and distribute easily through broth, vegetables, and sauces.

Because each piece is much smaller than penne or rigatoni, orzo has a high surface area relative to its size and picks up surrounding flavors readily.

The shape does not change the fact that it is pasta

Nutritionally and culinarily, classic orzo should be treated as wheat pasta. It contains gluten unless a specific product is made from alternative ingredients such as chickpea, corn, or another gluten-free base.

That also means it can be cooked in a large pot of salted water and drained exactly like other dried pasta.

Method 1: boil and drain

Barilla lists about 9–10 minutes for its classic orzo. Bring salted water to a boil, add the pasta, stir early in cooking, and taste before the final suggested minute to decide your preferred texture.

This method is especially useful for cold salads or whenever you want exact control over how much liquid remains in the finished dish.

Method 2: cook it directly in soup

Orzo's small size makes it a natural addition to broths and soups. It cooks directly in the liquid and releases some starch as it softens, slightly thickening the broth.

Remember that it keeps absorbing liquid after the heat is turned off. Soup stored with orzo can become much thicker by the next day.

Method 3: cook it “risotto-style”

Barilla also publishes recipes where orzo is sautéed and hot broth is added gradually until the pasta becomes tender and creamy. The finished dish resembles risotto visually even though the ingredient is pasta.

Starch released from the pasta surface thickens the surrounding liquid. Butter and cheese can enrich the final dish, but the creamy texture begins before those additions.

Do you need to rinse orzo?

Not before boiling it as pasta. Rinsing dry orzo removes little beyond surface dust and is generally unnecessary.

For cold salad, some cooks rinse after cooking to cool it rapidly and remove some surface starch, although that can make dressing cling less effectively. Spreading it out and dressing while still slightly warm is another option.

How do you keep orzo from sticking?

When boiling in plenty of water, stir during the first minute to separate the pieces. In an absorption-style preparation, stir periodically because the liquid becomes increasingly concentrated with starch as it reduces.

A small amount of oil after draining can help if the pasta must sit before being sauced, but it does not replace enough cooking liquid and movement during cooking.

Orzo vs. rice: when can you substitute?

The similar shape allows them to trade places in some dishes, but they do not behave identically. Rice absorbs water into the grain and varies in starch composition; orzo is gluten-containing wheat pasta.

The practical rule: when a package says classic orzo, think “small pasta,” not “rice.” Boil and drain it for salads, cook it directly in soup, or add broth gradually for a creamy risotto-style dish.

For repeatable results, use the same variety or brand and change only one variable at a time. Grain size, moisture, flour quantity, and cooking method can all change the final texture substantially, so your own reference is more useful than chasing one universal number.

faq.question: Is orzo rice?
faq.answer: No. Classic orzo is semolina pasta shaped like rice.

faq.question: How long does orzo take to cook?
faq.answer: A common reference is around 9–10 minutes, but package directions should take priority.

faq.question: Can you cook orzo like risotto?
faq.answer: Yes. It can be cooked by gradually adding broth until tender and creamy.
